abstract.text: As a promising branch of robotics, imitation learning emerges as an important way to transfer human skills to robots, where human demonstrations represented in Cartesian or joint spaces are utilized to estimate task/skill models that can be subsequently generalized to new situations. While learning Cartesian positions suffices for many applications, the endeffector orientation is required in many others. Despite recent advances in learning orientations from demonstrations, several crucial issues have not been adequately addressed yet. For instance, how can demonstrated orientations be adapted to pass through arbitrary desired points that comprise orientations and angular velocities? In this paper, we propose an approach that is capable of learning multiple orientation trajectories and adapting learned orientation skills to new situations (e.g., via-points and end-points), where both orientation and angular velocity are considered. Specifically, we introduce a kernelized treatment to alleviate explicit basis functions when learning orientations, which allows for learning orientation trajectories associated with high-dimensional inputs. In addition, we extend our approach to the learning of quaternions with angular acceleration or jerk constraints, which allows for generating smoother orientation profiles for robots. Several examples including experiments with real 7-DoF robot arms are provided to verify the effectiveness of our method.

sections.summary: The introduction frames the problem of learning and adapting Cartesian orientation, surveys DMP/TP-GMM/GMM/KMP approaches, and states the paper's four main aims: multiple quaternion trajectories, adaptation to quaternion/angular-velocity desired points, high-dimensional inputs, and smoothness constraints.
sections.title: Introduction and Problem Framing

source_span.start_text: II. PROBABILISTIC LEARNING OF QUATERNION TRAJECTORIES

sections.summary: This unit develops the probabilistic learning backbone: quaternions are mapped into Euclidean space via log(·), demonstrations are modeled with GMM/GMR to get a reference trajectory, and a kernelized KMP-style predictor learns quaternion trajectories from that reference.
sections.title: Probabilistic Quaternion Trajectory Learning

source_span.end_text: provided that Σ̃h is small enough⁸.

sections.summary: This unit explains how desired quaternion states and desired angular velocities are transformed into Euclidean space, encoded as additional reference points with covariances, and incorporated into the kernelized objective so that the adapted trajectory passes through arbitrary desired points.
sections.title: Adaptation to Desired Quaternions and Angular Velocities

source_span.start_text: IV. QUATERNION ADAPTATIONS WITH ANGULAR ACCELERATION/JERK CONSTRAINTS

sections.summary: This unit covers the analytical treatment of angular acceleration and jerk constraints, including the correspondence between minimizing ζ̈ or ζ⃛ and minimizing angular acceleration or jerk, the reformulated kernel objective, and the appendix derivation of the required kernel under acceleration constraints.
sections.title: Angular Acceleration and Jerk Constraints

source_span.end_text: both reproduction and adaptation issues can be directly tackled by using Dsr or DsrU.
source_span.start_text: V. LEARNING QUATERNIONS ASSOCIATED WITH HIGH-DIMENSIONAL INPUTS

sections.summary: This unit addresses quaternion learning when inputs are high-dimensional varying signals rather than time. It motivates the human-robot collaboration setting, samples inputs from a GMM marginal distribution to form a reference trajectory, derives the kernelized model, and extends it to desired-point adaptation.
sections.title: High-Dimensional-Input Quaternion Learning and Adaptation

sections.summary: The evaluation section reports simulated comparisons against orientation-DMP and TP-GMM, arbitrary via/end-point quaternion adaptations, angular-acceleration-constrained adaptation, rhythmic quaternion reproduction/adaptation, a real Barrett WAM painting task, and a KUKA human-robot handover task with high-dimensional inputs.
sections.title: Evaluations: Simulated and Real-Robot Tasks

sections.summary: The discussion reviews via-point/related work, states the limitations of Assumption 1 and the current focus on quaternion means rather than S3 covariance, proposes extensions, and concludes that the analytical approach enables broader orientation adaptation than prior target-only methods.
sections.title: Discussion, Limitations, and Conclusion

In contrast to [16] that learns quaternion displacements, the Riemannian topology of the S3 manifold was exploited in [17] to probabilistically encode and reproduce distributions of quaternions.
Moreover, an extension to task-parameterized movements was provided in [17], which allows for adapting orientation tasks to different initial and final orientations.
However, adaptation to orientation via-points and angular velocities is not provided.
Smoothness constraints

As suggested in [7], [22], the probability distribution of multiple demonstrations often encapsulates important motion features and further facilitates the design of optimal controllers [11], [23], [24], [25].
As a recently developed framework, KMP [8] exhibits several advantages over state-of-the-art approaches:
(i) In comparison with DMP [5] and TP-GMM [7], that focus on target adaptations, KMP is capable of adapting trajectories towards arbitrary desired points (e.g., start/via/end- points).
Angular acceleration/jerk constraints
We have successfully tested this solution in previous work on human-robot collaboration, namely in the collaborative hand task [8] and robot-assisted painting task [11], [34].
In [37], the task-parameterized DMP was studied, where the via-point constraint was handled as a task parameter vector.

relations.quote: As suggested in [7], [22], the probability distribution of multiple demonstrations often encapsulates important motion features and further facilitates the design of optimal controllers [11], [23], [24], [25].
relations.why: The probabilistic modeling and optimal-control mindset from these works provides the modeling basis for the proposed approach.

relations.quote: As a recently developed framework, KMP [8] exhibits several advantages over state-of-the-art approaches:
relations.why: The work builds directly on kernelized movement primitives and adapts that framework to quaternion orientation learning and adaptation.

relations.quote: (ii) Unlike DMP and ProMP [6] that rely on explicit definition of basis functions, KMP employs the kernel trick to alleviate the definition of basis functions and thus allows for convenient extensions to the learning and adaptation of demonstrations consisting of high-dimensional inputs.
relations.why: DMP/ProMP rely on explicit basis functions, while the proposed kernelized treatment is designed to avoid this limitation.

relations.quote: It is well known that robot trajectories should be smooth in order to facilitate the design of controllers as well as the execution of motor commands [20], [21].
relations.why: These references justify the need for smoothness constraints, which the paper incorporates into quaternion learning and adaptation.

relations.quote: In contrast, we propose to consider high-dimensional varying signals (e.g., human hand positions/orientations) as inputs and predict robot motions (e.g., Cartesian positions and orientations) according to the sensed states of the human hand.
relations.why: The proposed high-dimensional-input formulation is contrasted with time-driven human-robot collaboration approaches that require phase estimation or synchronization.

relations.quote: In order to cope with the via-quaternion and via-angular velocity constraints, the strategy of sequencing different DMPs was proposed in [18].

sections.summary: The introduction frames the problem of learning and adapting Cartesian orientation, surveys DMP/TP-GMM/GMM/KMP approaches, and states the paper's four main aims: multiple quaternion trajectories, adaptation to quaternion/angular-velocity desired points, high-dimensional inputs, and smoothness constraints.
sections.title: Introduction and Problem Framing

source_span.start_text: II. PROBABILISTIC LEARNING OF QUATERNION TRAJECTORIES

sections.summary: This unit develops the probabilistic learning backbone: quaternions are mapped into Euclidean space via log(·), demonstrations are modeled with GMM/GMR to get a reference trajectory, and a kernelized KMP-style predictor learns quaternion trajectories from that reference.
sections.title: Probabilistic Quaternion Trajectory Learning

source_span.end_text: provided that Σ̃h is small enough⁸.

sections.summary: This unit explains how desired quaternion states and desired angular velocities are transformed into Euclidean space, encoded as additional reference points with covariances, and incorporated into the kernelized objective so that the adapted trajectory passes through arbitrary desired points.
sections.title: Adaptation to Desired Quaternions and Angular Velocities

source_span.start_text: IV. QUATERNION ADAPTATIONS WITH ANGULAR ACCELERATION/JERK CONSTRAINTS

sections.summary: This unit covers the analytical treatment of angular acceleration and jerk constraints, including the correspondence between minimizing ζ̈ or ζ⃛ and minimizing angular acceleration or jerk, the reformulated kernel objective, and the appendix derivation of the required kernel under acceleration constraints.
sections.title: Angular Acceleration and Jerk Constraints

source_span.end_text: both reproduction and adaptation issues can be directly tackled by using Dsr or DsrU.
source_span.start_text: V. LEARNING QUATERNIONS ASSOCIATED WITH HIGH-DIMENSIONAL INPUTS

sections.summary: This unit addresses quaternion learning when inputs are high-dimensional varying signals rather than time. It motivates the human-robot collaboration setting, samples inputs from a GMM marginal distribution to form a reference trajectory, derives the kernelized model, and extends it to desired-point adaptation.
sections.title: High-Dimensional-Input Quaternion Learning and Adaptation

sections.summary: The evaluation section reports simulated comparisons against orientation-DMP and TP-GMM, arbitrary via/end-point quaternion adaptations, angular-acceleration-constrained adaptation, rhythmic quaternion reproduction/adaptation, a real Barrett WAM painting task, and a KUKA human-robot handover task with high-dimensional inputs.
sections.title: Evaluations: Simulated and Real-Robot Tasks

sections.summary: The discussion reviews via-point/related work, states the limitations of Assumption 1 and the current focus on quaternion means rather than S3 covariance, proposes extensions, and concludes that the analytical approach enables broader orientation adaptation than prior target-only methods.
sections.title: Discussion, Limitations, and Conclusion
